title: Top-K with a heap

glossary.definition: A continuous flow of data where you process elements one by one, often too large to fit in memory.
The minimum value required to enter a top-K list. In a size-K min-heap, the root acts as this threshold.

hook.scenario: You are processing a live stream of 10 billion financial trades and need to identify the 10 highest-value transactions.
hook.question: You can't fit 10 billion items in memory to sort them. How do you track the top 10 in a single pass?

why_it_exists.problem: Finding the `K` largest elements by sorting the entire array takes `O(n log n)` time. If you only care about a tiny subset `K`, sorting everything is massive overkill. Quickselect can find the top `K` in `O(n)` average time, but it requires holding the entire array in memory and modifying it.
why_it_exists.naive_solution: Sort the entire array in `O(n log n)` and slice the top `K`, or use a size-`n` Max-Heap and extract `K` times. Both are inefficient if `K` is much smaller than `n`.
why_it_exists.better_idea: Maintain a min-heap of size exactly `K`. As you stream through the data, push elements into the heap. If the heap exceeds size `K`, pop the minimum. By the end, the heap contains exactly the `K` largest elements, achieved in `O(n log K)` time and `O(K)` space.

mental_model.intuition: You are hosting a VIP club that only allows 10 people. If an 11th person wants to enter, they must be richer than the poorest person currently inside. A min-heap perfectly keeps track of that 'poorest person' at the root.
mental_model.description:
To find the `K` LARGEST elements, use a MIN-heap. Fill the min-heap until it has `K` elements. For every subsequent element, compare it to the root of the min-heap (the smallest of your current top `K`).

If the new element is larger, it kicks out the root: pop the root and push the new element. If it's smaller, ignore it. At the end, the heap holds the `K` largest elements, and the root is the `K`th largest.
mental_model.repeated_decision: Is this element bigger than the heap's root (the smallest of my current top-K)? If yes, pop the root and push it; if no, skip it.

explanation:
The Top-K pattern is the gold standard for processing massive data streams where `n` is too large to fit in memory. For frequency problems, you must count occurrences using a Hash Map, though this strictly requires the number of *unique* items to fit in memory. Once counted, you stream those frequencies into the min-heap.

The trick is entirely in the inversion: to find the `K` **largest** items, you must use a **min-heap**. Your primary administrative task is defending the boundary of your top-`K` list, so you need to constantly access the smallest element currently in your elite group. A min-heap perfectly keeps this exact eviction threshold sitting at the root, accessible in `O(1)` time.

Algorithm:
1. Initialize an empty min-heap and fill it with the first `K` elements of the stream.
2. For each remaining element, compare it to the root of the min-heap.
3. If it is larger than the root, pop the root and push the new element.
4. If it is smaller or equal, ignore it entirely.
5. After the stream ends, the min-heap contains the `K` largest elements.

Because the heap never exceeds size `K`, every push/pop operation costs at most `O(log K)`. Processing `n` elements yields a worst-case time of `O(n log K)`, but frequently skips elements in `O(1)` time. The memory footprint is strictly bounded to `O(K)`, making it perfect for infinite streams.

key_points.title: `K` Largest = MIN-Heap
key_points.detail: Use a min-heap to track the `K` largest items, because you need fast access to the smallest of those top `K` to evict it. (Conversely, use a max-heap for the `K` smallest items).

key_points.title: Complexity
key_points.detail: Time: `O(n log K)`. Space: `O(K)`. Highly efficient when `K` << `n`.

key_points.title: Stream processing
key_points.detail: This algorithm processes elements one by one, meaning the dataset does not need to be loaded into memory all at once.

pattern.name: Top K Elements
recognition_cues: The problem asks for the 'top `K`', '`K` largest', '`K` smallest', or '`K` most frequent' elements.
The input is a stream of data or too large to fit in memory.

engineering_examples.title: Analytics Leaderboards
engineering_examples.problem: Twitter tracking the Top 10 Trending hashtags among billions of real-time posts.
engineering_examples.why_this_algorithm: Frequencies are aggregated, and a size-10 min-heap acts as a filter, dropping anything that doesn't beat the 10th place hashtag.

engineering_examples.title: Database LIMIT queries
engineering_examples.problem: A SQL database executing `ORDER BY x LIMIT 10` on a billion-row table.
engineering_examples.why_this_algorithm: The database engine will often use a size-10 heap to scan the rows without ever attempting to sort the full billion-row table.

when_not_to_use.scenario: You have the entire array in memory and `K` is very large (e.g., `K` = `n`/2).
when_not_to_use.reason: Quickselect can find the `K`th element in `O(n)` average time and partition the array around it, which is faster than `O(n log K)` if the array is fully static in memory.

common_mistakes.title: Using a max-heap for the `K` largest
common_mistakes.explanation: This is the most common interview trap. Building a max-heap is `O(n)` and popping `K` elements takes `O(K log n)`, making the time `O(n + K log n)`. The fatal flaw is the `O(n)` space, which fails entirely on massive infinite streams.

common_mistakes.title: Sorting first
common_mistakes.explanation: Sorting takes `O(n log n)` time. For small `K`, `O(n log K)` is vastly superior, and sorting fails entirely if the data is a stream.

common_mistakes.title: Forgetting to cap the heap at size `K`
common_mistakes.explanation: If you don't pop when the heap exceeds `K`, the heap grows to size `n`. You lose the `O(K)` space advantage and the time complexity degrades to `O(n log n)`.

recall_questions.q: Which type of heap do you use to find the `K` largest elements?
recall_questions.answer: A min-heap, limited to size `K`. The root tracks the smallest element of the current top `K`, making it easy to evict.

recall_questions.q: What is the time and space complexity of the Top-K heap algorithm?
What happens if a new element is smaller than the root of the size-`K` min-heap?
recall_questions.answer: It is completely ignored. It is not large enough to crack the top `K`.

oa_questions.question: How would you find the `K` most frequent words in a massive text file?
oa_questions.answer: First, assuming the number of unique words fits in memory, use a hash map to count the frequencies. Then, iterate over the map and push the (frequency, word) pairs into a min-heap of size `K`, comparing by frequency. The final heap contains the top `K` words.
oa_questions.approach: Combine a frequency map with the Top-K heap pattern.

oa_questions.question: When would you choose Quickselect over a Top-`K` heap?
oa_questions.answer: Quickselect is better (`O(n)` average time) when the entire data set is statically available in memory and modifying the array is allowed. The heap is better for streams, read-only data, or when strict `O(K)` memory is required.
oa_questions.approach: Contrast online/streaming processing with offline/in-memory processing.
